bp: This paper studies a very small-looking decision that stands in for many web and marketplace problems: one opportunity appears now, later opportunities are unknown, and saying no cannot be undone. The story is hiring a single secretary from candidates who arrive one by one in random order, but the same shape appears whenever a system must accept or reject a streamed offer before seeing the rest of the stream. The company wants the hired candidate to have high value, yet it never sees the full list at decision time. Classical work asks for a multiplicative comparison with the best candidate that hindsight would choose, producing the familiar 1/e law. This paper asks a different practical question: if every candidate value is scaled between 0 and 1, how many value points can the online rule lose in the worst case compared with hindsight? That absolute loss is regret, and the paper builds selection rules around lowering it.
wh: The hard part is that waiting and acting are both dangerous for opposite reasons. If the company hires early, it may discover later that much stronger candidates were still coming. If it waits too long, the best candidate may already have passed and cannot be recalled. The random arrival order helps, because early candidates are a sample of what the stream might contain, but it does not reveal future values. The older competitive-ratio view also hides a practical tension. A ratio can make sense when values vary wildly, but when every value is normalized between 0 and 1, a company may care more about the absolute number of value points it leaves on the table. Losing 0.6 of a normalized value is a very different promise from losing 0.25. The paper is hard because it changes the yardstick, then must design and prove policies for the new yardstick.
naive: A smart beginner might copy the classical rule: ignore an initial fraction of candidates, remember the best value seen there, then hire the first later candidate who beats that remembered value. This is natural because the early sample gives a rough standard without spending the hiring slot. It fails under the regret yardstick because the rule was tuned for a ratio guarantee, not for a bounded absolute gap. The abstract states that the 1/e law has regret 1 - 1/e, about 0.632, even though values lie between 0 and 1. That means the rule can still be far from the hindsight best in the worst case. A second naive rule, using one fixed cutoff value, also fails because the right standard should change as time runs out.
ap: The paper's central move is to judge online selection by additive regret and then use pricing curves as the decision language. A pricing curve can be understood as a time-dependent acceptance price: at each point in the arrival process, the current candidate must be valuable enough to be worth spending the one hiring opportunity. Early in the stream, the price can be stricter because many candidates remain. Later, the price can fall because the option to wait is becoming less useful. The paper shows that this family can guarantee regret at most 1/4, and that this is the best possible guarantee within that class. It also studies a narrower best-only version, where the rule depends on the best candidate seen so far, and shows an even smaller guarantee of at most 0.190, with a lower bound of 0.171. The point is not just a new rule, but a new measurement of what good online hiring means.
mech: The input is a sequence of candidate values, each revealed only when that candidate arrives. The order is assumed uniformly random, so the position of a candidate in the stream is not chosen by an adversary after seeing the policy. The policy watches the stream one value at a time. At each arrival, it has the current time position, the values already seen, and the fact that only one hire can be made. A pricing-curve policy turns that state into an acceptance threshold, like a reservation price. If the current candidate clears the relevant price, the policy hires and stops. If not, it rejects the candidate forever and moves to the next arrival. After the whole thought experiment is complete, analysis compares the expected value earned by the policy with the value of the best candidate that hindsight could have selected from the full sequence. The regret is the worst-case additive gap between those two quantities, after values are normalized to the 0 to 1 range. The authors then prove upper bounds for policy classes: no pricing-curve algorithm in their class needs lose more than 0.25, best-only pricing curves can get to 0.190, and no policy of any kind can push the guarantee below 0.152. The mechanism therefore has two layers: the online rule for acting, and the proof that the rule's worst possible absolute loss is bounded.
math: The main mathematical idea is online decision-making under incomplete information. The chooser sees only the past and present, while the comparison point is an all-seeing hindsight chooser that knows every value. That mismatch creates regret: a number measuring how much value the limited-information rule gives up. Here regret is additive, meaning it is a direct subtraction between hindsight value and expected policy value, not a ratio. Normalizing values between 0 and 1 makes that subtraction meaningful across instances, because the largest possible value scale is fixed. Probability enters through the uniformly random arrival order. The values themselves can be difficult, but their positions are random, so an early sample has usable information about the stream without revealing everything. A pricing curve is a mathematical function from time, and possibly past observations, to an acceptance standard. It encodes the tradeoff between selectiveness and scarcity of remaining chances. Worst-case analysis asks for a guarantee that holds against the hardest value sequence allowed by the setup, not just an average easy case. Tightness and lower bounds are also central: saying 0.25 is tight within pricing curves means the analysis is not merely failing to find a better curve; within that rule family, a stronger promise is impossible. The general 0.152 lower bound says even unrestricted policies face a fundamental information limit.
dots: This paper belongs with online selection algorithms, but it also connects to several recurring conference ideas. It is a ranking problem compressed into a single irreversible choice: many candidates have values, yet the system can keep only one. It is also a sequential decision problem, like regret-based bandit and routing papers in the repo, because the policy must act before all evidence arrives and is judged by the loss from not knowing enough soon enough. The connection to optimization is the design of a decision rule that minimizes a clearly defined bad outcome, here worst-case additive regret. Unlike recommendation or retrieval papers that can show several items and learn from repeated user feedback, this setting has one slot and no recall. Unlike graph or language-model papers, there is no rich structure among items; the structure is temporal. That simplicity is useful: it isolates the cost of making an irreversible online decision under a random order.
ww: The pricing-curve idea works better than the naive classical rule because it matches the new loss measurement. Under additive regret, the question is not only whether the policy captures a constant fraction of the best value. It is how far, in normalized value points, the expected hire can fall below hindsight. A curve can express the changing value of waiting. At the beginning, rejecting a merely decent candidate is less costly because many chances remain. Near the end, the same rejection is more dangerous because the stream is nearly exhausted. By moving the acceptance standard over time, the policy balances two mistakes: spending the hire too cheaply and preserving the hire until it becomes useless. The best-only variant adds a grounded reference point from the observed stream: the best value so far tells the policy something about what counts as strong in this instance. The regret proofs matter because this intuition could otherwise be accidental. The stated upper and lower bounds show where the improvement is real, where a policy class has reached its limit, and where no online rule can beat the information barrier.
po: The payoff is a sharper guarantee for one-shot online selection when values are bounded. The classical 1/e law has regret about 0.632 under this additive view, while pricing curves guarantee at most 0.25, and best-only pricing curves guarantee at most 0.190. The paper also gives lower bounds, including 0.171 for the best-only class and 0.152 for all policies, so the result maps both what the proposed rules can achieve and what no rule can achieve. Practically, it gives designers of streamed selection rules a clearer promise: not just a fraction of hindsight, but a maximum absolute value gap under the model.
limits: The claims depend on the formal secretary setting in the abstract. Candidates must arrive in uniformly random order, the company must hire only one, decisions must be irrevocable, and values must be normalized between 0 and 1 for the additive regret numbers to mean what they say. Real hiring or marketplace selection may have correlated arrival order, strategic candidates, multiple hires, interviews that reveal noisy rather than exact values, or legal and fairness constraints not represented by a single value. The abstract reports theoretical guarantees for pricing-curve classes and lower bounds, but it does not show deployment evidence, user costs of false rejection, or how to choose among the other objectives mentioned at the end.
